title: Harnessing large-scale human omics data to decode novel risk genes for AD and its neuropsychiatric symptoms
text:
Approximately 90% of Alzheimer's disease (AD) patients experience neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS-AD)
that can contribute to greater functional impairment, higher caregiver burden, and earlier institutionalization.
Current treatments for AD and NPS-AD have limited efficacy but carry risk of adverse side effects,
underscoring the urgent need for safe and effective alternatives. To nominate targets for therapeutic studies,
we propose to functionally validate these AD/NPS-AD risk proteins in iPSC-derived cortical organoids, focusing
on their roles in AD and NPS-AD, including pathology, neuroinflammation, synaptic functions, and protein
expression networks.

title: Quantification of Low-Frequency Oscillations in Cerebrospinal Fluid Dynamics with Rapidly Acquired Tagging MRI and Learning-based Spatiotemporal Pattern Recognition
text:
This project aims to develop a novel Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) approach integrated with deep
learning based image analysis to accurately quantify movement of the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) in the human
brain. Once developed, this imaging framework can be employed to deepen our understanding of the
physiological drivers of CSF flow and how it clears waste products from the brain. The findings may lead to
earlier detection and better treatment of hydrocephalus, Alzheimer’s disease, and related conditions.

title: Leveraging primary cell and organoid culture to identify and map the human virome
text:
Despite years of study, human susceptibility to chronic disease is still not fully understood, compelling the
continued search for modifiable risk factors. One previously hidden variable is the human virome, a vast array of
viruses that reside within the body without causing overt symptoms, but which may impact susceptibility to many
common diseases, ranging from autoimmunity to cardiovascular disease to cancer. This project will develop new
technologies to accurately observe, characterize, and quantify the human virome, with the long term goal of
discovering new ways to prevent and treat common diseases.

title: Integrating Clinical, Pathologic, and Immune Features to Predict Breast Cancer Recurrence and Chemotherapy Benefit
text:
Nearly one in eight women will develop a diagnosis of breast cancer over the course of their lifetime, and
selection of treatment is often based off a gene expression assay such as OncotypeDX. Deep learning can
integrate readily available clinical, pathologic, and immune features to predict recurrence and chemotherapy
benefit, resulting in more accurate, faster, and cost-effective treatment decisions.

title: Mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation in substance use disorder and HIV
text:
This research aims to enhance treatments for HIV-associated neurocognitive disorders (HAND)
in individuals with opioid addiction—especially those using fentanyl—by targeting mitochondrial
dysfunction and neuroinflammation. Utilizing innovative human organoid models and an HIV-Tg
rat self-administration model, the study will assess the therapeutic potential of NAD+ to restore
cellular energy metabolism and mitigate HAND, fentanyl dependence, and withdrawal symptoms.
Ultimately, these advances could lead to novel interventions that improve health outcomes,
extend life, and reduce the burden of chronic disease among vulnerable populations with HIV and
opioid use disorder.

title: The genetic origins of vertebrate evolutionary novelties: the fin-to-limb transformation
text:
Evolutionary novelties are structurally and functionally novel traits in animal diversification.
Despite their functional significance in animal survival and diversification, evolutionary and
developmental mechanisms of novel body plans remain mostly unknown. The long-term goal of
this proposal is to identify the genetic origins of evolutionary novelties and understand how
anatomically and functionally integrated organs originate during animal evolution.

title: Project II: Immune regulatory circuits in primary colon cancer and lymph node and liver metastases
text: Project II. Immune regulatory circuits in primary colon cancer and lymph node and liver metastases Experimental Lead: Rudensky Computational Lead: Leslie Experimental Co-Lead: Ganesh PROJECT SUMMARY Colorectal cancer (CRC) represents the third most common cancer in the US and worldwide. Despite major advances in treatment of some cancer afforded by immunotherapy, mismatch repair-proficient (pMMR) CRC, which accounts for the vast majority (85%) of cases, fails to respond with ~15% 5-year survival rate. We hypothesize that this failure is due to the activity of CRC-promoting local circuits of immune and stromal accessory cells, in which suppressive regulatory T (Treg) cells and non-inflammatory tissue-supporting Th17 cells serve as essential components. We also propose that the architecture and cellular composition of these T cell circuits are distinct in primary CRC and in proximal lymph node and distal liver metastases. In this project, we will dissect the dynamics of the main immunomodulatory cells states including Treg and Th17 cell and their interactions with cellular components (“immunomodulatory neighborhoods”) in primary tumors and lymph node and liver metastases in the same pMMR CRC patients alongside a novel mouse genetic model of spontaneously metastasizing pMMR CRC (Aim 1). Our perturbation studies will elucidate roles of these key immunomodulatory cells and their partners in metastatic disease progression and resistance to immunotherapy (Aim 2) and examine the impact of key immune cell-derived factors on cancer cells in human primary and metastatic CRC organoids (Aim 3). We will employ cutting edge “omics” analyses at a single cell resolution combined with spatial transcriptomics and highly multiplexed optical imaging and microscopy and flow cytometry coupled to experimental perturbations iteratively with novel computational modeling and analyses to deconstruct archetypal T cell-based cell circuits in CRC and conserved chromatin states and gene regulatory programs of their cellular constituents. These studies will enable better mechanistic understanding of emergence of pro-metastatic cell states in pMMR CRC and inform development of orthogonal rational combination immunotherapies for this disease and elucidate the therapeutic actionability of targeting immune-epithelial circuits in preventing and treating metastasis in patients with advanced CRC. .

title: Michigan Center for Urban African American Aging Research - Analysis Core (AnC)
text: REVISED Analysis Core (AnC) Abstract The overarching goals of the Analysis Core (AnC) are to support innovative research into social and behavioral processes underlying health problems, and to train junior investigators on the tools and approaches that will enhance the rigor of their research to generate meaningful insights regarding the health and well-being of older adults. The objectives of the AnC are twofold. The first objective is to provide MCUAAAR Scientists, and Center faculty with the methodological and analytical tools necessary to conduct and complete pilot projects and RCMAR-related research in a manner that is both transparent and rigorous. This objective involves providing training, consultation, and logistical support in (a) state-of-the-art approaches to study design, data collection, and data analysis, and (b) NIH best-practices in rigor and reproducibility, including study pre-registration, coding and documentation, and data sharing. The second objective is to embed collaborative, interdisciplinary team science into research practice through a thematic, case-based training framework informed by the biopsychosocial model. Collectively, these objectives seek to generate novel scientific insights and methodological approaches to reduce health problems and promote well-being of African Americans over the life course. The AnC has expertise and experience supporting a wide range of projects (i.e., primary data collection, secondary data analysis, mixed-methods designs, advanced statistical techniques, and machine learning tools) and provides a forum for Scientists to gain meaningful exposure to methods from a wide range of disciplinary orientations. The AnC objectives leverage long- standing, mutually-beneficial relationships with the other MCUAAAR Cores, networks of NIA, NIH and University centers, organizational partners, and initiatives at UM, WSU, and MSU that have a shared commitment to applied social and behavioral science and to mentoring junior investigators. We fully expect, based on our prior interactions, that the analytic methods and training tools developed by the AnC will be shared within the MCUAAAR, with the RCMAR Coordinating Center and NIA and NIH collaborating centers, organizational partners, and the broader scientific community.

title: Rewired Signaling at the Nexus of Melanoma Metastasis and Resistance
text:
Leveraging discoveries emerging from our previous R35, this proposal extends findings relevant to rewired UPR
signaling affecting tumor-intrinsic (ATF4 pro- and anti-apoptotic signaling) and -extrinsic (microbiota composition
and anti-tumor immunity) pathways. We propose to study these processes during aging, which provide
unprecedented opportunity to study melanoma metastasis, thus offering novel paradigms to address
fundamental unanswered questions in cancer biology.

title: The Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) for Cancer Research
text:
Given the enormous amount of data generated by research studies and in the clinic today, visualization is often
a key element in gaining insight into the genomic basis and mechanisms of disease. These insights will help to
develop hypotheses for further study, guide treatment, and point the way to new therapeutic targets. We propose
to ensure that the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) continues to track and respond to advances in genomics
technology and changing user needs, and maintains its high level of utility for the cancer research community.

title: Role of obesity in blood pressure regulation and insulin resistance in Polycystic Ovary Syndrome
text:
Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS) is a common health condition that affects about 10% of women of
reproductive age. Women with PCOS have elevated levels of the male androgen hormone testosterone and a
high prevalence of obesity, insulin resistance, and elevated blood pressure, which lead to cardiovascular
disease. This proposed research will shed light on novel androgens-mediated mechanisms that will translate
into effective and safe therapeutic agents to treat the cardio-metabolic complications frequently found in
women with PCOS.

title: Hawaii Pacific Islands Mammography Registry
text:
The proposed studies are relevant to public health because they have the potential to identify women at high
risk of breast cancer using ethnic-specific models. Thus, this advance is expected to have a high impact to the
health and well being of women because women at high risk may choose to alter the breast cancer screening
frequency for earlier detection or to participate in risk reduction strategies, such as lifestyle modification. Both
approaches will reduce breast cancer mortality. This is relevant to the part of NIH's mission which focuses on
the prevention of disease by supporting research in the prevention and early detection of human diseases.

title: AS160 as a nodal regulator of the cardiac response to metabolic stress
text:
Obesity and metabolic disorders are increasing in epidemic proportions in the country which ultimately leads to
poor outcomes including heart failure. AKT substrate of 160kDa (AS160) has been identified as nodal regulator
between insulin signaling and glucose uptake, but research into its physiological role in cardiomyocyte
metabolism has been hampered by limitations of available models. In this context, our studies are focused on
elucidating the composition of the cardiac AS160 regulatory complex, how this complex and AS160 regulation
is altered during disease, and the effect on cardiomyocyte metabolism in order to develop novel therapeutic
strategies for cardioprotection in obesity and obesity related metabolic syndromes.

title: Innovating next generation technologies to define mechanisms of neurodegenerative disease and devise therapeutic strategies
text:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and other neurodegenerative diseases are
devastating for individuals and families involved; there are no cures and few treatments.
Our studies have revealed new insights into the major ALS protein TDP-43, defined a
new genetic risk factor for ALS – mutations in the ataxin 2 gene, validated it as a
therapeutic target, and discovered that cryptic splicing in the UNC13A gene explains
why variants in this gene increase risk for ALS. The proposed studies will use
genomewide approaches to reveal regulators and therapeutic targets to lower
neurodegenerative disease proteins, single-cell transcriptomics to define mechanisms
of motor neuron degeneration, and exploring additional TDP-43 cryptic splicing targets,
laying the foundation for the development of novel therapeutic approaches.

title: SPARKLED: Do After School Programs Affect Risk in Kids of Latent Endothelial Disease
text: Heart problems are the number one cause of pregnancy-related death in the United States. After school care can help children lead healthier lives by teaching them about stress management and healthy diets, which can help prevent heart disease later in life. Our research project studies how after school care for teenagers can empower communities across the United States to overcome barriers to health and reduce the long-term burden of heart disease during pregnancy.

title: Structural and Functional Studies of the TRPM4 and TRPM5 Channels
text:
TRPM4 and TRPM5, which are Ca2+-activated, nonselective, Ca2+-impermeable, voltage-gated ion channels,
play key roles in cerebral artery constriction, immune response, insulin secretion, taste and temperature
sensation, and are thus critically linked to cardiovascular diseases, diabetes, and transduction of taste stimuli.
This research project will focus on the temperature-dependent gating mechanism of TRPM4 and TRPM5 and
their pharmacology, taking advantage of single-particle cryo-EM and electrophysiological recording. The
proposed research is relevant to public health and NIH’s mission, because the work will provide a deeper
understanding and knowledge of the relationships between atomic structure and function in the temperature-
modulated TRPM family members, as well as a foundation for developing new drugs for cardiovascular diseases
and diabetes.

title: Host-environment interactions in the pathophysiology of digestive disease
text:
OVERALL
Research supported through the WU DDRCC has and will continue to have a profound impact on understanding
the pathophysiology of digestive disease and the role of host-environment interactions. The WU DDRCC
promotes scientific collaboration and diversity of our research base to identify new therapeutic opportunities with
the potential for rapid translation into clinical trials for patients with digestive diseases.

title: Columbia University-Weill Cornell Medicine CFAR (CU-WCM CFAR)
text:
The Columbia University (CU) – Weill Cornell Medicine (WCM) Center for AIDS Research (CFAR) brings
together researchers from 2 major institutions united by a single large hospital system in New York City to
catalyze and promote HIV research; foster new collaborations; provide robust services to faculty and community
members engaged in HIV research; and develop the careers of new investigators entering the HIV field. The
CU-WCM CFAR will promote HIV basic, translational, clinical, behavioral, implementation and outcomes
research with a regional, national, and international impact and the overall goal of ending the HIV epidemic.

title: Evolution of influencer-driven e-cigarette marketing on social media and its effect on e-cigarette perceptions and use patterns among adolescents
text: Micro-influencers promoting e-cigarettes on social media on behalf of tobacco brands have been increasingly using audio-visual effects, including stylizing themselves to appear younger, depicting e-cigarettes in positive lifestyle contexts (e.g., healthy lifestyle), and incorporating sounds that evoke pleasant sensations, all of which may contribute to normalization of e-cigarette use. To understand the impact of common marketing tactics used by these influencers, the proposed study will 1) conduct two randomized between-subject experiments among 6,000 (per each experiment) U.S. adolescents and an eye-tracking within-subject experiment among 300 adolescents to test effects of audio-visual features on perceptions of influencer credibility, e-cigarette harm perceptions, appeal, and susceptibility to e-cigarette use (Aim 1), and 2) detect and monitor influencers’ use of these audio-visual marketing features on social media over time (2019-2029), using computer vision (Aim 2). The goal of this project is to inform the field about adolescents’ risks of exposure to harmful influencer-driven e-cigarette-related content on social media, which can lead to more effective tobacco prevention and cessation interventions for adolescents.

title: Cancer Center Administration
text: CANCER CENTER ADMINISTRATION - ABSTRACT Administration at the Karmanos Cancer Institute (KCI) provides support to the Cancer Center leadership, Research Program and Shared Resource infrastructure, KCI membership, and staff by providing services aimed at relieving the administrative burden associated with research. Administration contributes to the mission of the Cancer Center by providing efficient management of resources, facilitating key internal and external scientific meetings, strategic planning, and developing useful metrics to aid in the decision making of KCI senior leadership. Mr. Evano Piasentin, Associate Center Director for Research Administration, leads an experienced administrative team. Administration supports 135 scientific members across four research Programs and nine Shared Resources (including one under development). Additionally, Administration manages extramural funding of $63 million (annual direct costs), KCI’s annual research budget of $21 million, and coordinated internal pilot funding of more than $2 million since the last renewal. Notable achievements during the past funding period include a restructuring of the administrative office to capitalize on the unique skills of staff and provide a more efficient and dynamic environment to meet the needs of the Cancer Center. Additionally, Administration supported the planning, process, and development of a new strategic plan through organization of strategic planning retreats convening stakeholders from various disciplines across KCI. The strategic plan is centered on five priority areas: immunology and immunotherapy, cancer metabolism and metabolomics, biology of cancer health disparities, addressing multilevel determinants of risk and survivorship, and increasing interventional research to reduce disparities. Administration continues to implement significant upgrades to the Research Administration Application (RAA©), a homegrown repository of CCSG data for KCI. With respect to space management, Administration managed a relocation of basic science laboratories from the outdated Prentis Cancer Research Building to the renovated Elliman Research Building. Finally, Administration played a central role in the development of several large, multi-PI project grants leading to the first-ever funded SPORE grant at KCI; The Michigan Prostate SPORE (P50CA186786).
